html:
Byzantine Iconoclasm was the struggle over holy images in the Byzantine Empire, in two periods, from about 726 to 787 and from 815 to 843. Emperors and their bishops banned icons, the painted images of Christ, Mary and the saints, and treated those who honoured them as idol worshippers.

  • First period. Leo III is said to have removed an image of Christ from the palace gate around 726 or 730. His son Constantine V made the ban church law in 754 and persecuted the monks who resisted.
  • First restoration. Empress Irene called the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which restored icons.
  • Second period. Leo V brought the ban back in 815 after defeats by the Bulgars. It lasted until Emperor Theophilos died in 842.
  • Final restoration. His widow Theodora restored icons in 843, a victory the Orthodox church still celebrates.

Why it began is still argued. Some point to Arab victories read as God's punishment, others to Islamic and Jewish bans on images, or to a wish to curb the monks. John of Damascus wrote the main defence of icons: since God had become visible in Christ, Christ could be painted.
